summary.text: If primes \(p,q\) have different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither divides \(d\), then \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some index among the first 150 makes \(a+id\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\), a contradiction. Applying this to selected pairs among \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17\) forces \(2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\mid d\) and either \(11\mid d\) or \(13\mid d\), hence \(d\ge2310>2025\).

full_proof.text:
Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there cannot exist integers \(a\ge 2\) and \(1\le d\le 2025\) for which all of
\[
 a,
+d,
+2d,
+\cdots,
+149d
\]
are lopsided. This disproves the stated existence conjecture.

We begin with the key modular observation.

**Lemma.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be primes whose final decimal digits are different, and suppose that \(pq\le 150\). If every one of the 150 terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), is lopsided, then
\[
 p\mid d\quad\text{or}\quad q\mid d.
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** Suppose, to the contrary, that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Because \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid d\), we have \(\gcd(d,p)=1\); likewise \(\gcd(d,q)=1\). The primes \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct, since their final digits differ, and consequently
\[
 \gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). Therefore the congruence
\[
 a+id\equiv 0\pmod{pq}
\]
has a solution modulo \(pq\), namely
\[
 i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq},
\]
where \(d^{-1}\) denotes the inverse of \(d\) modulo \(pq\).

Choose the unique representative \(i\) of this residue class satisfying
\[
 0\le i<pq.
\]
Since \(pq\le 150\), this index satisfies \(0\le i<150\), so \(a+id\) is one of the given 150 terms. The congruence says that \(pq\mid a+id\), and hence both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). Moreover, \(a+id\ge a\ge 2\), so this term is nonzero and \(p,q\) really are among its prime divisors. But the final digits of \(p\) and \(q\) are different. Thus \(a+id\) has prime divisors with two different final decimal digits and is not lopsided, contrary to the hypothesis. This proves the lemma.

We now apply the lemma to a finite list of small prime pairs. All the numbers
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17
\]
used below are prime. For each displayed pair, its two members have different final digits and their product is at most \(150\). Hence the lemma gives the following alternatives:
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
(2,3):&2\mid d\text{ or }3\mid d, & 2\cdot3=6,\\
(2,5):&2\mid d\text{ or }5\mid d, & 2\cdot5=10,\\
(2,7):&2\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d, & 2\cdot7=14,\\
(2,11):&2\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d, & 2\cdot11=22,\\
(2,13):&2\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d, & 2\cdot13=26,\\[2mm]
(3,5):&3\mid d\text{ or }5\mid d, & 3\cdot5=15,\\
(3,7):&3\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d, & 3\cdot7=21,\\
(3,11):&3\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d, & 3\cdot11=33,\\
(3,17):&3\mid d\text{ or }17\mid d, & 3\cdot17=51,\\[2mm]
(5,7):&5\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d, & 5\cdot7=35,\\
(5,11):&5\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d, & 5\cdot11=55,\\
(5,13):&5\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d, & 5\cdot13=65,\\[2mm]
(7,11):&7\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d, & 7\cdot11=77,\\
(7,13):&7\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d, & 7\cdot13=91,\\[2mm]
(11,13):&11\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d, & 11\cdot13=143.
\end{array}
\]
For clarity, the final digits in the less immediate cases are: \(11\) ends in \(1\), \(13\) ends in \(3\), and \(17\) ends in \(7\). Thus every pair listed indeed has distinct final digits.

We will repeatedly use two elementary divisibility facts. First, if coprime positive integers \(r\) and \(s\) both divide \(d\), then \(rs\mid d\). In particular, if several distinct primes divide \(d\), their product divides \(d\). Second, because \(d>0\), any positive divisor \(m\) of \(d\) satisfies \(m\le d\). Consequently, exhibiting a divisor of \(d\) larger than \(2025\) contradicts \(d\le 2025\).

We next show successively that \(2,3,5,7\) must all divide \(d\).

First suppose that \(2\nmid d\). The five alternatives obtained from the pairs
\[
(2,3),\ (2,5),\ (2,7),\ (2,11),\ (2,13)
\]
then force
\[
3\mid d,
\quad 5\mid d,
\quad 7\mid d,
\quad 11\mid d,
\quad 13\mid d.
\]
These are distinct primes, so their product divides \(d\):
\[
3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=15015\mid d.
\]
Since \(d>0\), this implies \(15015\le d\), contradicting \(d\le2025\). Therefore
\[
2\mid d.
\]

Next suppose that \(3\nmid d\). The alternatives from
\[
(3,5),\ (3,7),\ (3,11),\ (3,17)
\]
force
\[
5\mid d,
\quad7\mid d,
\quad11\mid d,
\quad17\mid d.
\]
We already know that \(2\mid d\). Hence the product of the five distinct primes \(2,5,7,11,17\) divides \(d\):
\[
2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090\mid d.
\]
This gives \(13090\le d\), again contradicting \(d\le2025\). Thus
\[
3\mid d.
\]

Now suppose that \(5\nmid d\). The alternatives from
\[
(5,7),\ (5,11),\ (5,13)
\]
force
\[
7\mid d,
\quad11\mid d,
\quad13\mid d.
\]
Together with the already established divisibilities \(2\mid d\) and \(3\mid d\), this implies
\[
2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=6006\mid d.
\]
It follows that \(6006\le d\), which is impossible because \(d\le2025\). Therefore
\[
5\mid d.
\]

Finally, suppose that \(7\nmid d\). The alternatives from
\[
(7,11),\ (7,13)
\]
then give
\[
11\mid d\quad\text{and}\quad13\mid d.
\]
Since \(2,3,5\) have already been shown to divide \(d\), the product
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290
\]
divides \(d\). Hence \(4290\le d\), contradicting the upper bound on \(d\). We conclude that
\[
7\mid d.
\]

We have proved
\[
2\mid d,
\qquad3\mid d,
\qquad5\mid d,
\qquad7\mid d.
\]
Since these primes are distinct, their product divides \(d\):
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210\mid d.
\]
Apply the lemma one last time to \(11\) and \(13\). Their final digits are \(1\) and \(3\), and \(11\cdot13=143\le150\), so
\[
11\mid d\quad\text{or}\quad13\mid d.
\]
There are two cases.

* If \(11\mid d\), then \(210\) and \(11\) are coprime and both divide \(d\). Therefore
  \[
  2310=210\cdot11\mid d.
  \]
  As \(d>0\), this implies \(2310\le d\), contradicting \(d\le2025\).

* If \(13\mid d\), then similarly
  \[
  2730=210\cdot13\mid d,
  \]
  and hence \(2730\le d\), again contradicting \(d\le2025\).

Both alternatives are impossible. Therefore no positive common difference \(d\le2025\), and no starting value \(a\ge2\), can produce 150 consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression all of whose prime divisors share the same final decimal digit. The proposed arithmetic progression does not exist.
